newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Cash-crunch talk puts Vietnam banks in spotlight.
newsitem.headline: Cash-crunch talk puts Vietnam banks in spotlight.

text.p: The financial health of Vietnam's private banks has come under scrutiny this week following a report that one of the fledgling sector's best-known institutions failed to honour a deferred letter of credit.
"The government has been flagging its worries about joint-stock (privately-owned) banks for months," said one foreign banker on Friday. "Now it looks like some problems are coming home to roost."

VP Bank, the first non-state-owned commercial bank to take foreign shareholders, said there were inaccuracies in an Asia Times report that the bank had defaulted on a $3 million letter of credit for a shipment of steel from South Korea's Ssangyong Corp.
A VP Bank official, who declined to be named, said there were "no major problems" with the deal.
But she stopped short of denying that the bank had failed to meet its payment deadline.
Vietnam Joint-Stock Commercial Bank for Private Enterprises (VP Bank) in 1995 became the first private bank to have foreign shareholders.
Those shareholders, each of which hold a 10 percent stake, are the Dublin-listed Vietnam Fund and Dragon Capital, which is part of the Dublin-listed Vietnam Enterprise Investments Ltd.

"We are happy shareholders of VP Bank now, but we are not in a position to comment on the workings of the bank at the present time," said John Shrimpton, a partner of Dragon Capital in Ho Chi Minh City. "We are basically very happy shareholders."
The bank, based in Hanoi, has capital of 250 billion dong ($22.32 million) and reported a profit of 76 billion ($6.79 million) in 1996.

"It would not be surprising if some of the banks were having cash-flow problems," said a source who had seen an audit of VP Bank's 1995 accounts. He said the bank had decided not to request an audit of its 1996 books.
One industry source said the letter of credit agreement had been happily resolved and that the chief difficulty facing the bank now was internal squabbling at management level.
The central State Bank of Vietnam, which regulates the banking system, has declined to comment on the situation.
However, it has made clear in recent months that it is concerned about the precarious financial health of some of the 52 joint-stock banks.

Hanoi, which began reforming the economy along market lines in the late 1980s, created four big state-run commercial banks out of the central bank in 1990. A host of smaller joint-stock banks, owned by private shareholders, sprang up after that.
However, the joint-stock banks have struggled to compete and many are believed to have dangerously high levels of overdue debt, partly due to a wave of deferred letter of credit deals in early 1996.
Two joint-stock banks agreed in December to merge in a bid to bolster their capital base, and State Bank of Vietnam deputy governor Do Que Luong has said others may follow suit.
